Lemon olive oil marinated chicken, kale and parmesan kale whole wheat pasta, and blistered cherry tomatoes
I'd be interested in a more complete recipe, if you don't mind...

Sure:

Chicken:

Ingredients:

  • 1/4 olive oil
  • 1/4 cup lemon juice
  • 3 cloves garlic. minced (or to your taste)
  • 1/2 tbsp dried oregano
  • 1/2 tsp salt (or to your taste)
  • Fresh cracked pepper (need to use fresh, not pre-cracked)
  • 1-1.5 lbs boneless skinless chicken breasts (or chicken thighs - depending on size you might need more marinade)

Add oil, lemon juice, garlic, oregano, salt and pepper to large zip bag. Close bag and massage to combine the ingredients. Filet each breast into two thinner pieces. I like to pound them out a little bit to make them a bit thinner and more tender. Place them in the bag, making sure the chicken is covered in the marinade. Marinate for at least one hour to 24, turning occasionally to maximize the contact with the marinade.

To cook, heat a large skillet over medium flame, then transfer the chicken (two pieces at a time to reduce juice pools that prevent browning). 5-7 minutes each side. Discard the excess marinade.

Let the chicken rest for five minutes before slicing.

Pasta:

Ingredients:

  • 1 bunch kale
  • 1/2 lb angel hair pasta (i like whole wheat for this recipe)
  • 2 tbsp olive oil
  • 2 tbsp butter
  • 2 cloves garlic, minced (or to taste)
  • 1/4 cup grated parmesan (don't go cheap, get the real thing and freshly grate)
  • Pinch of salt and fresh cracked pepper to taste
  • Red pepper flakes if you desire

Remove the kale leaves from the stems and tear or cut into 2-inch pieces. Rinse the dale well under cool water and let it drain. Bring your water for noodles to a boil, add it to the boiling water, and cook al dente (about 7 min). Drain the pasta. While the pasta is cooking, add the olive oil and butter with the garlic to a skillet. Cook over medium flame for about 1-2 min. Add the kale and continue to saute until the gale has wilted and turns deep green (5-7 min). Turn off the heat and add the drained pasta to the skillet. Toss these two together and then allow it to cool. You want it to be warm but not warm enough to melt your cheese. Add additional seasoning to taste.

Tomatoes:

One container of cherry tomatoes is all you need. When the chicken has finished cooking, add theses directly to the skillet and cook over medium flame for 3-5 min or until the tomatoes are blistered. You can add a small amount of water if needed to deglaze the pan slightly to add more flavor, although it is not necessary.

Enjoy.

Due to my size (5'7" and 145 pounds with gray hair), people don't see me as physically threatening, although I've been told many times that I'm intellectually intimidating (absurdly high IQ), but once people get to know me they figure out that I'm a genuinely nice guy and I use my giftedness to help people (although if you're in an enemy military unit that's squaring off against one I'm in, you're likely to have a very bad day). Enough about me: I just needed to set the stage for what I do when people come to me for advice about weight and fitness.

For the past 37 years I've been associated with the military in one fashion or another. From my first day as a cadet to my current status as a field-grade officer in the Retired Reserve, I've always been within the military's weight standards. Only once did I even fail a PT test (just the running event: I was nursing a knee injury, plus it was as hot as Tarzan's balls the day I tested - I passed the re-take a few days later). Nonetheless, I was a little heavier and doughier than I needed to be when I was getting to the end of my career. When I retired I took a civilian job training soldiers, and I really didn't want to turn into yet another military retiree with a big gut... I never respected those guys when I was in uniform and I had too much self-respect to go down that road myself (plus I wanted the health benefits of being in shape). Over the course of a couple of years I went from "meh" to "Holy Crap!"... and not only do people notice, by they frequently comment now. (It is one the great ironies of my existence that I get female attention - even occasional admiration - now that I've been married for 30 years when I was practically invisible to women when I was single.)

I've learned two things over all those years of people asking for advice: 1) most people want their problems to be fixed but they aren't willing to put in a lot of effort to fix them, and 2) you can't help someone who doesn't want to be helped. I'll add a third insight I got from a friend of mine who's a professional counselor, "Don't work harder on somebody's problem than they're willing to work on it themselves."

All that being said, I occasionally get asked questions like, "How do you do it, Colonel Avocado?" in reference to my physical condition. I'm usually a "sweet as pie" guy in person, so I don't come off as a douche-canoe when I just lay it out for them in blunt terms. I tell them that I have some physical challenges, but the bottom line is that I make time to exercise - a lot - and eat a balanced diet. That's it. That gives them an "out" if they want it, because they can always say, "I don't have that kind of time."

Fine: I understand that not everyone lives within walking distance of a gym, nor has the wherewithal to work out every day. If someone wants an excuse to fail, nothing I say is going to prevent that, so I serve one up for them on a platter. (Why waste time on someone who's not serious about changing?) But like I said, I'm a genuinely nice guy, so I offer them a way out if they're willing to take it. I say that I'm certified as a personal trainer and I'm willing to give them some help if they want it. I don't even charge for it: I didn't get certified to make money, but because I wanted the knowledge for myself and I want to be able to help (mostly) my fellow veterans.

When they tell me that they can't devote the kind of effort that I do (they all say that - and in most cases it's probably true), but they still want to work on it, I offer to do a full-body assessment to get them started. I tell them to carve out about three hours for me to evaluate everything about them. If you study to be a personal trainer they'll tell you that a lot of people don't like to be evaluated like that (since it puts their years of failure on display), but I stress that it's not about me making a judgement, but simply the only means by which I can customize a plan to suit their particular situation. (I've found that people tend to jump at the chance to have a head-to-toe evaluation.) I tell them that getting in better shape is going to take time, but they need to realize that they didn't get fat overnight, and they're not going to get back into fighting trim overnight, either. I tell them that they have the rest of their life to get better... that "health" requires a permanent lifestyle change and is not something that comes from a temporary change... that they need to understand that anything is better than nothing, and more is better than less (short of causing an injury)... and that 80% of their success will come from the grocery aisle rather than the gym.

It's like the time/distance problems we all learned how to solve in elementary school math class: D=RT. The further you have to go or the slower you go, the longer it's going to take, but a long as you keep making progress you'll get closer. In the case of health it's Goal = Effort x Time. Even the fattest fatty can do something, and every step (as long as they don't sabotage it by "rewarding" themselves all the time) equals progress back toward normality.

That's how I deal with it. Make the person understand that getting better is a journey made up of thousands of tiny (and extremely manageable) steps... and that while there are no shortcuts, and it doesn't require a lifetime of single-minded focus, either.
